text: Lesson eighty-four, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE. Chapter ten, Window and Ranking Functions.

FIRST_VALUE of name, over partition by color order by list price descending, as most expensive in color. This returns the name of the FIRST row in each window, according to the order by inside OVER — here, the most expensive product name for that color, attached to every single row in the partition, not just the first one.

Now here's the one almost everyone gets wrong the first time. LAST_VALUE of name, same partition and order by, as supposedly cheapest in color. Run it, and that column is almost always just the CURRENT row's own name — not the actual cheapest product in the color. This isn't a bug. It's the default frame doing exactly what it's defined to do.

Here's why. Every window function has a frame — we'll cover that properly next lesson — and when you add an order by inside OVER without specifying one, SQL Server applies a default frame: range between unbounded preceding and current row. That means everything from the start of the partition up to and including the current row. So from LAST_VALUE's point of view, the last row it can see IS the current row, every single time.

The fix is an explicit frame. Rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following. That tells SQL Server the frame is the ENTIRE partition — everything before the current row, and everything after it. Now LAST_VALUE actually returns the cheapest product name in that color, every time, instead of silently repeating the current row. FIRST_VALUE never had this problem, by the way — the true first row is always inside that default frame. It's only the true last row that usually falls outside it.
Next lesson: Window Frames, ROWS versus RANGE — the frame clause you just saw, explained properly from the ground up. See you there.
